public_rationale: The scored core is whether, from October 2024 to March 2025, vendors ran benchmarks on test sets they could see, with informal or no safeguards against training on them. OpenAI open-sourced SimpleQA on 2024-10-30, and its announcement reports results for its own models (e1). In January 2025, an Epoch AI co-founder said OpenAI had access to FrontierMath and had a 'verbal agreement' not to train on its problem set (e2). He said Epoch also kept a separate holdout set as a safeguard for independent verification (e2). Epoch's lead mathematician said Epoch could not vouch for OpenAI's o3 score until its independent evaluation was complete (e3). The cited sources from the period do not describe a binding audit, enforceable rule, or penalty against training on test data. Zitron makes no accusation of cheating, so no proven case is needed. His general point that honor systems often fail at high stakes is not scored. In April 2025, after the post, LMArena said Meta's reading of its policy did not match its expectations and that it was updating its leaderboard policies (e4). That is outside the period and is context only.
limitations: The general maxim that honor systems 'often don't work' at high stakes is not scored. 'Often' and 'real consequences' have no stated standard.
The evidence covers SimpleQA and FrontierMath, not every benchmark or vendor.
The absence of binding audits or penalties rests on the cited sources not describing any. The packet does not survey all benchmark governance in the period.
The SimpleQA source (e1) shows the test set was public. It does not itself discuss safeguards against training on it.
Two items (e2, e3) come from one news report quoting Epoch AI staff.
Whether reputational damage counts as a 'real consequence' is a matter of judgment.
The evidence does not show whether Epoch's holdout check was later completed or what it found.

statement.excerpt: There’s an honor system, and honor systems often don’t work when there’s billions of dollars on the line, and there’s no real consequences for actually cheating.

our_interpretation: The checkable core is two factual statements. First, vendor-reported scores on benchmarks like SimpleQA rest on trust: the vendor runs the test, the answers are public or available to it, and no independent check confirms it did not train on them. Second, no binding rule or penalty enforces against such cheating.
The line 'honor systems often don't work when billions are on the line' is a general maxim, not a fact about AI. It is not scored on its own.
Zitron explicitly makes no accusation of actual cheating. So support does not require any documented case of cheating.
Target period: from SimpleQA's public release (October 2024) to the post date (2025-03-24). This is the state of benchmark practice he describes in the present tense.
criteria.support_condition: Sources from the target period show benchmark results that vendors run themselves, on test sets they can see, with only informal or no safeguards against training on the test (for example, an unwritten agreement and no independent check).
criteria.contradiction_condition: Sources show that during the target period major vendor benchmark results were subject to binding independent audits, enforceable rules, or penalties against training on test data.

evidence.excerpt: We hope that open-sourcing SimpleQA drives the research on more trustworthy and reliable AI forward
evidence.explanation: The SimpleQA questions and answers are open to anyone, including the vendors who report scores on it. Nothing described here stops a vendor from tuning on the answers, so honest results depend on trust.

evidence.excerpt: while OpenAI has access to FrontierMath, it has a “verbal agreement” with Epoch AI not to use FrontierMath’s problem set to train its AI.
evidence.explanation: For a leading math benchmark, the only safeguard against OpenAI training on test problems it could see was a verbal agreement. That is an honor system with no formal enforcement.

evidence.excerpt: “However, we can’t vouch for them until our independent evaluation is complete.”
evidence.explanation: The benchmark's own lead mathematician said OpenAI's reported score rested on trust and had not been independently verified. This matches Zitron's point that outsiders can't easily tell whether a vendor cheated.

evidence.excerpt: Meta should have made it clearer that “Llama-4-Maverick-03-26-Experimental” was a customized model to optimize for human preference. As a result of that we are updating our leaderboard policies
evidence.explanation: After the post, a vendor's leaderboard entry was publicly challenged. The response was a public statement and a policy update, not a formal penalty. This falls outside the target period, so it is context only.
